title: The page is open
hook: women study Talmud today; communities differ about how

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siyum: finish the page, then promise to return. This week laid the table and its cloth, made the law clear, met new questions, put life first, kept arguing, and threw a party at the end of a book. Today, who gets to open it. Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

Some rough neighbors were making Rabbi Meir's life miserable, the Talmud says, so miserable that he prayed they would die. His wife, Beruriah, stopped him. What are you basing this on? He pointed to a verse in the Psalms, let sinners cease out of the earth. She told him to read it again. The Hebrew can be read as sins, not sinners. Let sins cease. And look at the end of the verse: then the wicked will be no more. Pray that they turn back, she said, and there will be no more wicked. He did, and the Talmud says they turned back. A woman, reading closely, correcting a sage. Today's word starts there.
screen: `RABBI MEIR PRAYS AGAINST NEIGHBORS.` → `BERURIAH: READ IT AGAIN.` → `LET SINS CEASE, NOT SINNERS.`

segments.voice: The page is open. First, Beruriah. She appears in the Talmud by name, as a sharp reader of scripture, and her argument turns on a single word. The sages kept her reading on the page. Second, an old disagreement, kept honestly. The Mishnah in tractate Sotah records two views. Ben Azzai says a man is obligated to teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer objects, and says teaching a daughter Torah is like teaching her foolishness. Both views stay in the Mishnah, side by side, and later generations had to decide which one to walk by. Third, today. Women now study Talmud in classes, in study halls, with study partners, and in daily page-a-day cycles, and some have celebrated finishing the whole of it. Communities differ on this, and say so openly. Orthodox communities disagree among themselves about how and what women should study, with some building serious programs of Talmud study for women and others holding back. Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist movements teach Talmud to women and men alike, including in rabbinic training. Fourth, the page itself. In Hebrew, a page of Talmud is a daf. Remember the Vilna edition: the same page everywhere. Open a particular daf in any study hall and the same lines are waiting. The page doesn't check who opened it. It just asks to be read closely, the way Beruriah read.
screen: `BERURIAH, READING CLOSELY.` · `BEN AZZAI AND RABBI ELIEZER.` · `TODAY: STUDY HALLS AND DAILY PAGES.` · `THE SAME PAGE, FOR WHOEVER OPENS IT.` · then, large: `THE PAGE IS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to encourage one learner. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who is learning something right now. A child with homework. A friend in a new job. A parent figuring out a new phone. Someone who started late and feels it. See them at their table, page open. Now find one sentence you could say that would make them want to keep reading. Not advice. Encouragement. Hold the sentence, and let it get simpler. The bell holds the time.
The page is open. Women's study of Talmud today, in communities that differ about it, and a page, a daf, that asks only to be read closely. Today's word.
Your line: the page is open. Today, say your sentence to that learner, by message or in person, and leave the door open for a question. Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

screen: `DAY 1120 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOR THE WAYS OF PEACE.`

howItsDone: Women study Talmud in women's study halls, synagogue classes, university courses and daily page cycles, alone or with a study partner. Communities differ in what they offer and encourage.
